title: Flooded street or yard in Vero Beach? What to do now that the county is under a state of emergency
seoTitle: Vero Beach Flooding: What to Do After the Emergency
description: Monday's rain flooded Vero Beach streets and put the county under a state of emergency. What happened, what to do about septic, wells and wet rooms.
dek: Heavy rain on Monday, Nov. 2, flooded streets and yards across Vero Beach. The county and the state both declared emergencies, and schools are closed today. Here is what homeowners should do in the next few days, especially if you are on septic or a well.
facebook: Is there still water in your street, your yard or your swale this morning? Vero Beach got hit hard on Monday. Here's what the state of emergency means, why you shouldn't pump your septic tank yet, and what to do in the first 48 hours if water got inside.

what to do after house floods Vero Beach

body.text: If you woke up to water still sitting in your street, your swale or your yard, you are not alone. Monday, Nov. 2, brought round after round of heavy rain to Vero Beach. By late afternoon, the National Weather Service in Melbourne said 5 to 11 inches had already fallen across southeastern Indian River County, including Vero Beach, Vero Beach South and Gifford, with more possible.

This article covers what happened, what the emergency orders mean, and the steps that matter most for your house this week. If water got into your home, or you are on septic or a private well, read the last three sections closely.

body.title: The short version
body.text: Indian River County declared a local state of emergency at 2:30 p.m. Monday. It stays in effect until further order. Gov. Ron DeSantis also declared a state of emergency for seven counties, including Indian River. Indian River County schools are closed today, Tuesday, Nov. 3. Do not drive through flooded roads. If you are on septic, do not have the tank pumped while the ground is soaked. If your well flooded, drink bottled or boiled water until it is tested.

The rain came in waves all day. News crews photographed cars driving through flooded parts of Royal Palm Boulevard near First Presbyterian Church, and a van pushing through water on Indian River Drive near the Vero Beach Dog Park. CBS12 reported water covering roads, front lawns and driveways in several neighborhoods, including around 41st Avenue and 12th Street.

The county said numerous roads had become impassable. TCPalm reported that 58th Avenue SW between 13th Street SW and 17th Street SW was closed until further notice, with only emergency and local traffic allowed. All five county customer convenience centers (the drop-off sites for trash and recycling) were closed Monday. At the beach, parts of the Conn Beach boardwalk were closed after erosion.

County Administrator John A. Titkanich Jr. signed the local emergency order, which took effect at 2:30 p.m. Monday. Later that day, the governor declared a state of emergency for Brevard, DeSoto, Hardee, Highlands, Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties. That order also lets local elections offices move polling places that flooding has made unsafe or hard to reach.
Stay off flooded roads, even familiar ones

The sheriff's office shared a photo of an SUV with only its roof showing above the water and urged everyone to stay off the roads. The county asked residents to obey every road closure and barricade. The weather service message is short: turn around, don't drown. You cannot see whether the road under the water is still there.

The coast is rough too. A High Surf Advisory for coastal Indian River County called for breaking waves of 5 to 6 feet, and a high rip current risk runs through late Tuesday night. Stay out of the water.
If your home is on septic

This is where well-meaning homeowners make expensive mistakes. When the ground is soaked, your drainfield cannot take water. The Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County told residents not to have septic tanks pumped while groundwater is this high, and to conserve water if plumbing is slow.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency gives the reason: pumping a tank in saturated ground is only a temporary fix, and an empty tank can float up out of the ground and break its pipes. The EPA also says to keep cars and equipment off the drainfield while the soil is wet, and to have the tank pumped and checked once the water goes down if you see signs of damage, like the system settling or not taking water.
If you are on a private well

If floodwater covered your wellhead, or you are not sure, health officials say to use bottled or boiled water for drinking, making ice, brushing teeth and cleaning cuts until the well is tested. The Florida Department of Health in Indian River County handles private well questions at 1900 27th St., Vero Beach, phone 772-794-7440. Its page reminds owners that keeping well water safe is the property owner's job.

The clock matters. The CDC says to clean and dry wet items, or remove them, within 24 to 48 hours after water gets in, to keep mold from growing. Do not touch flooded electrical or mechanical equipment until it is dry and clean. If sewage backed up into the house, the EPA says to disinfect those areas with a solution of half a cup of bleach per gallon of water. Avoid contact with floodwater, especially with an open cut, and wash any wound well with soap.

items: Stay home if you can, and never drive around a barricade.
Walk your property in daylight. Look for water at the foundation, in the garage and around the AC closet.
On septic? Use as little water as you can, skip laundry for now, and do not pump the tank until the ground dries out.
On a well that flooded? Use bottled or boiled water and call the health department at 772-794-7440 about testing.
If water got inside, open up and dry out within 24 to 48 hours. Pull wet rugs and cardboard boxes first.
Keep kids and pets out of standing water and away from storm drains and ditches.

Voting today? Polls are open 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Some polling places in the county were moved because of flooding, so check voteindianriver.gov or call the Supervisor of Elections at 772-226-4700 before you go.

body.text: Sebastian Daily, citing the weather service, reported that conditions should improve midweek, with more sunshine by Thursday. Until the water drains, treat any road with water on it as closed.

faq.q: Is Indian River County under a state of emergency?
faq.a: Yes. The county declared a local state of emergency at 2:30 p.m. on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, and it stays in effect until further order. The governor also included Indian River in a state of emergency for seven flooded counties.

faq.q: Are Indian River County schools closed because of flooding?
faq.a: Indian River County schools are closed Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, according to the Florida Department of Education list reported by Florida Today.

faq.q: Should I pump my septic tank after a flood?
faq.a: Not while the ground is still soaked. Health officials say to wait until groundwater goes down. Pumping a tank in saturated soil can let it float and break its pipes. Conserve water until then.

faq.q: Is my well water safe after flooding in Vero Beach?
faq.a: If floodwater reached your well, use bottled or boiled water until it is tested. Call the Florida Department of Health in Indian River County at 772-794-7440.

faq.q: How fast do I need to dry out my house after water gets in?
faq.a: The CDC says to clean and dry wet items, or remove them, within 24 to 48 hours to help prevent mold.
